title: Overhaul steering system components on agricultural equipment

lessons.title: How tractor steering works and finding faults
lessons.html:
Types of steering

Farm tractors use one of two main steering types:

  • Mechanical steering – older and small tractors. The steering wheel turns a steering box. The box moves a drop arm, drag link and tie rods that turn the front wheels.
  • Hydrostatic (power) steering – most modern tractors. The steering wheel turns a steering valve (orbital unit). Hydraulic oil from a pump goes to a steering cylinder that turns the wheels. There is no solid link between the wheel and the front axle.

Both types have tie rod ends (ball joints), king pins or pivot bushes, and the front axle pivot.

Signs of steering faults

SignPossible cause
Too much free play in the wheelWorn tie rod ends, worn steering box, loose bolts
Heavy steeringLow oil, weak pump, dry king pins, low front tyres
Tractor wanders on the roadWrong toe-in, worn joints
Steering wheel turns by itself or driftsLeaking steering cylinder seals or valve
Uneven front tyre wearWrong toe-in, bent tie rod

Why this matters

Steering is a safety system. A tractor that cannot steer properly can roll on a slope, go into a dam or hit a person. A tractor with a steering fault must not be used on the farm or on a public road until it is fixed. Report steering problems at once.

lessons.title: Overhauling steering parts safely
lessons.html:
Preparing

  1. Park on level ground, switch off, take out the key and chock the back wheels.
  2. Jack up the front and put it on axle stands. Never work under a tractor on a jack alone.
  3. Read the manual for the steering system. Get the seal kits, new tie rod ends and split pins.
  4. For hydrostatic steering: release the pressure as the manual says before opening any pipe. Clean around fittings first and cap open pipes so dirt does not get in.

Tie rod ends

  1. Remove the split pin and nut.
  2. Use a ball-joint separator to free the joint. Do not hammer the thread.
  3. Count the turns as you unscrew the old end, then screw the new one on the same number of turns. This keeps the toe-in close.
  4. Fit a new nut or split pin and tighten to the manual torque.

Steering cylinder

  • Remove the cylinder and drain the oil into a tray.
  • Take it apart on a clean bench as the manual shows.
  • Check the rod for scratches and bends, and the bore for scoring.
  • Fit a new seal kit. Lubricate seals with clean hydraulic oil.

King pins and bushes

Check for play by rocking the wheel top and bottom. Replace worn pins and bushes and grease them until fresh grease shows.

Never straighten a bent steering arm or tie rod by heating it. Replace it with a new part.

lessons.title: Setting toe-in and testing the steering
lessons.html:
Setting toe-in

Toe-in means the front of the front wheels is a little closer together than the back of the wheels. It helps the tractor run straight and stops tyre wear. The manual gives the toe-in value for your tractor.

  1. Put the wheels straight ahead on level ground.
  2. Measure between the front tyres at hub height, in front of the axle.
  3. Measure at the same height behind the axle.
  4. The difference is the toe-in. Adjust the tie rod length until it is correct.
  5. Tighten the lock nuts.

Bleeding hydrostatic steering

After work on hydrostatic steering, fill the tank with the correct oil. Start the engine and turn the steering wheel slowly from full left to full right several times to push air out. Top up the oil level. Air in the system makes the steering jerky.

Testing

  • Check free play at the steering wheel is within the manual limit.
  • Turn lock to lock. The steering must be smooth with no tight spots.
  • Check for oil leaks at the cylinder, pipes and valve.
  • Check the wheels do not touch anything at full lock.
  • Do a slow test drive in the yard with your supervisor. The tractor must run straight and return easily.

Record the work, the parts and the toe-in measurement on the job card.

Key points

  • Steering is a safety system; a faulty tractor must not be used.
  • Support the front on axle stands and release hydraulic pressure before opening pipes.
  • Replace bent steering parts – never heat and straighten them.
  • Set toe-in to the manual value and tighten lock nuts.
  • Bleed air from hydrostatic steering and test before use.

quiz.question: In hydrostatic steering, what turns the front wheels?

options.text: A chain from the steering wheel
A steering cylinder moved by hydraulic oil

quiz.question: Too much free play in the steering wheel is often caused by what?
Why do you count the turns when unscrewing an old tie rod end?

options.text: To know how long the job takes
To keep the toe-in close when fitting the new one

quiz.question: What should you do with a bent tie rod?

options.text: Hit it straight with a hammer
Leave it if the tractor still steers
Replace it with a new part

quiz.question: How do you remove air from hydrostatic steering after repair?

options.text: Turn the wheel slowly lock to lock with the engine running, then top up
Open all pipes with the engine off
Let the air out of the front tyres
